title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
Setting: p = P is an odd prime with primitive root a, so the powers 1, a, a^2, …, a^{p-2} run through all nonzero residues mod p. In the theorem on the previous page Euler writes any x not divisible by p as x ≡ a^λ, so x^2 ≡ a^{2λ}. Hence every nonzero quadratic residue is an even power of a.

Corollary 1 (§52): the set of nonzero quadratic residues mod p equals the set of residues of the progression 1, a^2, a^4, a^6, …

Corollary 2 (§53): write p = 2n+1. Since gcd(2, p−1) = gcd(2, 2n) = 2, a^2 is not a primitive root. So the squares do not give a complete residue system.

Corollary 3 (§54): a^{2n} = a^{p-1} is the least power of a congruent to 1. So the even powers a^0, a^2, …, a^{2n-2} are n distinct classes. There are therefore exactly n = (p−1)/2 nonzero quadratic residues and n non-residues. Euler recalls that he earlier named the latter 'non-residua'.

Scholion 1 (§55, continued on p.111): write the complete residue row 1, α, β, γ, δ, … under 1, a, a^2, a^3, …, a^{2n}. Then:
- the quadratic residues are the entries in even positions, 1, β, δ, ζ, …;
- the non-residues are the entries in odd positions, α, γ, ε, η, ….

The next page adds the observation that b^2 ≡ (p−b)^2, which explains why the 2n squares 1, 4, …, 4n^2 give only n distinct residues.

Purpose: the page re-derives the basic structure of quadratic residues from the primitive-root (index) viewpoint. This continues E449's programme of proving the residue theorems (Euler's criterion, the power-residue counts that follow on the next page) via primitive roots.
errors: None mathematically. Corollary 3 states the result loosely: the n residues come from the exponents 0, 2, …, 2n−2, with a^{2n} merely returning to 1. The argument also tacitly assumes that a primitive root exists. Euler's own existence proof elsewhere in E449 is known to be incomplete; Gauss later criticised this in Disquisitiones Arithmeticae §56.

ideas.what: Quadratic residues mod p are exactly the even powers of a primitive root.
ideas.modern_name: Index (discrete logarithm) characterization of quadratic residues; squares form the index-2 subgroup of the cyclic group (Z/p)^*.
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E449); systematized by Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), §§52–57 and §97ff.
ideas.where_published: E449 itself (Novi Commentarii Acad. Petrop. 18, 1774). Related material in Euler's residue papers, e.g. E262 and E271.

ideas.what: Exactly (p−1)/2 nonzero quadratic residues and (p−1)/2 non-residues for an odd prime p.
ideas.modern_name: Count of quadratic residues; index of the subgroup of squares.
ideas.where_published: Euler's earlier residue papers (e.g. E262), where the term 'non-residua' was introduced; E449 here.

ideas.what: a^2 is not a primitive root because gcd(2, p−1) ≠ 1.

deep.surprise_reason: Textbook material, well known and already credited to Euler: quadratic residues as even powers of a primitive root, and their count (p−1)/2. Nothing new for a specialist.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image. The superscripts in the progression 1, a^2, a^4, … are faint in the scan but correctly read. The last term in §55, a^{2n}, is correct.
